analysis.one_liner: Restores stricter civil rights standards for workplace discrimination lawsuits and extends those protections to congressional employees.
analysis.headline: The Senate's civil rights fix died in committee: introduced by Sen. Danforth with zero cosponsors, it was never voted on before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's 1989 Wards Cove decision weakened protections against employment practices that disadvantage racial minorities and women, this bill would have restored the older Griggs v. Duke Power standard. Workers claiming a seemingly neutral rule (like a test or hiring criterion) has a discriminatory effect would no longer have to prove the employer intended discrimination. It also bans adjusting test scores by race or sex, preserves employers' rules against illegal drug use, and — notably — applies these anti-discrimination rights to the Senate's, House's, and congressional agencies' own employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face hiring, promotion, or testing practices that screen out members of a protected group even without intent to discriminate. It also benefits the thousands of employees who work for Congress itself, who would gain Title VII-style rights for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing biased hiring and testing

how_it_helps.text: Restores the burden of proof from Griggs v. Duke Power: once a worker shows a practice causes a discriminatory impact, the employer must show the practice is required by business necessity.
Lets a worker win even when a practice is job-related, if a less discriminatory alternative exists and the employer refuses to adopt it.
Declares that the Wards Cove decision weakened federal civil rights protections and states the bill's purpose is to overrule it.
Extends anti-discrimination rights and remedies to employees of the Senate, the House, and congressional agencies like CBO and GAO.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — and labor organizations and joint training programs, which count as 'respondents' — would bear greater litigation risk and would need to validate hiring practices and consider less discriminatory alternatives. Congress itself would bear new liability for its own workplaces.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans employers from adjusting test scores or using different cutoff scores by race, sex, or other protected traits — a compromise that some civil rights advocates opposed, since race-norming had been used to counteract biased tests.

It confirms that employers may bar people who knowingly use or possess illegal drugs, and such a rule can only be challenged as intentional discrimination — a carve-out that limits claims by drug-using applicants.
The 'business necessity' standard requires only a 'manifest relationship' to the job, a threshold critics could argue is looser than the original Griggs standard.
Claims by Senate employees would be investigated and adjudicated by the Senate Ethics Committee, inside the chamber itself, rather than in court or before the EEOC.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have meaningfully strengthened workers' ability to challenge hiring practices that exclude women and minorities, at a real but bounded cost to employers in litigation and record-keeping. Its compromises — the test-score rule, the drug carve-out, and the Senate keeping enforcement of its own employees' claims in-house — show it was written to be passable, not maximalist.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1991 and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. John Danforth introduced the bill on June 27, 1991, with no cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever recorded.
The bill's stated purpose was to overrule the Supreme Court's Wards Cove decision and codify the earlier Griggs standard for disparate impact cases.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced stronger disparate impact lawsuits, and incumbent members of Congress who kept their own workplaces outside the ordinary enforcement system — until a later bill changed that.

for.name: Sen. John C. Danforth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and gave it its findings and purpose: overrule Wards Cove, restore Griggs.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in June 1991 and never reported it out, held no markup, and never sent it to the floor.

against.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee of jurisdiction that never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a senior Republican with zero cosponsors from either party and never received a hearing, markup, or vote, so no partisan split is recorded.

industries.industry: Employers (private businesses, and labor organizations and training programs as respondents)
industries.note: The bill shifts the burden of proof to employers to justify hiring practices with discriminatory effects, raising litigation exposure. For workers, that is the point: employers could no longer keep practices that exclude protected groups without strong justification.
Stronger business-necessity scrutiny would force validation of tests, but the bill also outlaws adjusting test scores by race or sex, which removes a compliance tool some testing programs had used.

industries.industry: Congress as employer (Senate, House, and congressional agencies)
industries.note: The bill applies Title VII rights to congressional employees, but the Senate would adjudicate its own employees' claims through the Ethics Committee, keeping enforcement inside the institution rather than in court.
